statement: Whether African early Homo erectus-attributed material should be classified as a separate species, Homo ergaster, distinct from Asian Homo erectus sensu stricto, remains a live and unresolved taxonomic debate, though the field appears to be trending toward treating both as one polytypic species.
scholarly_disagreement: Whether cranial/facial differences between African and Asian erectus-attributed material (sagittal keels, cranial vault thickness, robusticity) represent species-level distinction or normal intraspecific geographic variation.

sources.citation: Groves, C. & Mazák, V. Original erection of Homo ergaster, using KNM-ER 992 as type specimen.
sources.author: Groves, C. & Mazák, V.

sources.author: Antón, S.C.

interpretations.position: African material warrants separate species status as Homo ergaster

holders.name: Colin Groves & Vratislav Mazák
holders.work: Original 1975 naming, using KNM-ER 992 as type

interpretations.strongest_case: Phylogenetic/functional analysis finds African and Asian samples form distinguishable clades under cladistic methods.

interpretations.position: A single, polytypic Homo erectus sensu lato spanning Africa and Asia is preferable

holders.name: Susan Antón
holders.work: American Journal of Physical Anthropology 122(S37):126-170 and later syntheses

interpretations.strongest_case: No consistent, non-overlapping character suite cleanly separates the African and Asian samples; variation falls within normal range for a geographically dispersed hominin.

notes: Reported trend is toward the lumping position gaining ground, but Homo ergaster remains in active use in the literature, particularly for KNM-ER 992-type and Dmanisi-adjacent material.
